transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-11
Time: 15:00 - 15:55 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Gomez (AtlasRetail Eng Mgr), Owen Lee (AtlasRetail DevOps), Sophie Tran (AtlasRetail Product)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in for Dedicated sizing. Discussed autoscaling policies, burst capacity, QoS, and next steps.

00:00 Laura Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um quick check, can you hear me all right?
00:04 Maya Gomez: yes loud and clear, thanks laura
00:07 Laura Chen: awesome, so agenda today is a quick review of the test results from last week, then go into the autoscale policy options for the Dedicated pool and plan a sustained burst test. Ravi will lead on the metrics.
00:22 Ravi Patel: yeah i'll start, i pulled the logs from friday's load run — note that some of the tags were a bit off in the exporter so i patched them, but overall we saw the expected queue growth when we crossed 120 reqs per second. GPU util hit about 78% sustained on the primary node, and tail latency p99 jumped from 210ms to around 720ms when the KV cache miss rate went up.
00:45 Owen Lee: sorry can you repeat the p99 number? i missed that.
00:47 Ravi Patel: p99 to ~720ms, yeah — that's when the KV cache (i think exporter said K-V cash) missed and we started hitting model blank loads.
01:02 Sophie Tran: when you say queue growth, is that request queueing inside the Redwood runtime or at our side load balancer?
01:06 Ravi Patel: primarily inside the runtime; the request router was flat. We saw worker threads saturated and an increase in queue length for the inference queue. So end-to-end impact is the tail latency bump.
01:18 Maya Gomez: do we have request size distribution? most of our traffic is chat-ish, 800 to 1,200 tokens, but some background summarization jobs are longer.
01:26 Owen Lee: i put a quick histogram in the shared drive, it's rough but shows p50 ~420 tokens, p95 ~1,050, p99 ~2,300.
01:36 Ravi Patel: that matches the latency curve — longer sequences amplify memory pressure and KV cache churn. For Dedicated sizing we recommend sizing for p95 in steady state and setting burst policy to handle p99 spikes.
01:50 Laura Chen: ok that matches our previous guidance; let's talk autoscale policies. We have two knobs: target concurrency-based autoscale and utilization-based autoscale, plus burst credits for short spikes.
02:05 Ravi Patel: yes, target concurrency helps keep latency predictable — you pick a concurrency per GPU, e.g., 8 concurrent synth calls per GPU for your model variant. Utilization-based scales on GPU utilization threshold, good for throughput-optimized workloads. For AtlasRetail's mix i think a hybrid is best: target concurrency for normal chat traffic and a burst policy that allows temporary scale above committed nodes for short windows.
02:29 Owen Lee: how long is a "short" window? our holiday traffic is spiky for hours sometimes.
02:33 Ravi Patel: good question. Burst credits are designed for bursts up to a few minutes to an hour per event. For multi-hour sustained bursts (>1-2hrs) we recommend reserved burst capacity or temporarily increasing the committed pool, because the economics of burst credits get expensive and autoscaler can thrash.
02:50 Maya Gomez: so for our holiday promos, we'd probably need a plan to bump capacity in advance. can we script that?
02:55 Laura Chen: yes you can pre-schedule capacity changes and we also support canary rollouts and temporary overrides via API. We can also set autoscale cooldowns to avoid thrash.
03:07 Sophie Tran: what's the cost delta between committed nodes and burst credits? rough order of magnitude.
03:11 Laura Chen: ballpark, burst credits are priced at a premium — roughly 2x the committed per-hour rate in many cases — but that depends on the exact GPU type and term; we'll send exact numbers.
03:19 Ravi Patel: also note that quantization/packing choices matter — if you can accept int8-ish quality, you can pack more concurrency per GPU which reduces both steady-state and burst cost.
03:30 Owen Lee: our quality bar is strict for customer-facing chat; we might use quant for background summarization but keep high precision for front-end.
03:38 Maya Gomez: yes agreed.
03:40 Laura Chen: ok next, recommended Dedicated pool plans: given your p95 ~1,050 tokens and peak qps of about 150 during tests, a conservative starting pool is 4x A100-equivalent GPUs with target concurrency set to 6, and a burst window to allow scaling up to 8 GPUs for up to 60 minutes, with automated cooldowns of 10 mins.
04:02 Ravi Patel: right — the math: with concurrency 6 and average latency at p95 ~220ms for that token range, each GPU can handle ~27 qps steady, so 4 GPUs give ~108 qps steady capacity; burst to 8 GPUs covers short-term 216 qps. For sustained above that we advise provisioning more.
04:21 Owen Lee: that seems OK, our expected non-holiday peak is 120 qps so 4 GPUs is slightly under — maybe 5 GPUs steady?
04:27 Maya Gomez: i think we should target 5 committed to reduce reliance on burst credits.
04:31 Laura Chen: totally reasonable. we can model cost for 4 vs 5 committed and show burst credit spend for each. i'll include both in pricing.
04:39 Ravi Patel: one more operational note: prefix/KV caching can be warmed for common chat patterns. If you can surface common prefixes and user intents, we can reduce cache miss rate and tail latency.
04:51 Sophie Tran: we have some common templates for customer replies, we can share the top 50 after redaction.
04:55 Maya Gomez: we'll export them this week.
04:57 Owen Lee: question on failover — if Dedicated pool hits capacity and autoscaler can't scale fast enough, is there a fallback to hosted?
05:03 Laura Chen: yes, we support fallback policies: route to hosted 'best-effort' variant or throttle; we can set costs and latency SLOs per route. For your SLA we suggested fallback to hosted with degraded latency but better availability, during unexpected sustained overload.
05:18 Ravi Patel: add that routing incurs inter-region egress if done across regions, so keep routing local to region to avoid egress costs.
05:26 Maya Gomez: got it.
05:28 Sophie Tran: about the 3-hour sustained burst test you suggested, what's the exact plan?
05:32 Ravi Patel: plan is to run a ramp test on your staging traffic generator: ramp to target 180 qps over 15 minutes, sustain for 3 hours, capture per-GPU utilization, queue length, p50/p95/p99 latency, and KV cache hit/miss rates. We'll also enable detailed tracing for tail latencies.
05:52 Owen Lee: can we run it on Wed night? we have staging free then.
05:55 Laura Chen: wed night works for us; ravi i'll coordinate with you after the call to pick the slot.
05:59 Maya Gomez: one more ask — can you share a sample autoscale policy config so our infra team can review?
06:04 Ravi Patel: yep i'll drop a template in the shared drive, it's a JSON snippet with fields for target_concurrency, max_nodes, burst_window_mins, cooldown_secs, and quantization_profile. note the exporter sometimes garbles field names, but i'll include comments.
06:22 Laura Chen: ok let's recap next steps. Ravi runs the 3-hour sustained burst test Wed night and shares logs by Thu morning; Laura sends revised pricing and 4/5-committed models by Tue EOD; AtlasRetail exports token histograms and top prefixes by next Monday. We'll meet again to go over the burst test early next week.
06:45 Maya Gomez: sounds good, thanks all.
06:48 Laura Chen: thanks everyone, i'll send calendar for follow-up. bye.
06:52 transcript_end_notes: some minor transcription errors in product names (Redwoode in one log) and exporter tags; see attached logs and drive links.
